title: Paula and the Poof City
markdown:
The city was so enormous its buildings tickled the bellies of the clouds, and the air thrummed with a sound so constant you almost forgot it was there. Tuesday, until it wasn’t. The day the whole city went poof.

Paula taught people how to talk on the telephone, to sound sympathetic about things they had never heard of. Her trick was scripted empathy. With a few well-chosen phrases she could make you feel as warm as a hand-knitted jumper, all from a paragraph about customer service. She adored her tidy desk, her lined-up pens, her guidebooks of bullet points. Every frown ironed out by the right sentence. Every grumble smoothed by a timed apology. Her office was a quiet harbour where feelings were managed like delicate teacups, not truly felt.

Across town, in a dusty attic of wires, crackling records, and the faint aroma of burnt toast, lived Deniz. He was a pirate of the airwaves, broadcasting on a sneaky tinny frequency only the most determined ear could find. He detested scripts. Words were sparrows, meant to dip and dive, not sit in cages. He rambled, voice a warm rumbling tide of unadulterated him. The attic was a jumble of whirring contraptions and half-eaten biscuits, a kingdom of spontaneity.

Then the city’s electronic heart sputtered and died. Lights blinked out. Screens went black. The hum dissolved into a vast unnerving silence. Paula’s phrases turned brittle, dry leaves in an empty room, utterly useless. Her neat world crumbled, leaving her adrift. The old dread coiled in her stomach: a tight knot, fear of the unplanned, the messy, the real. She looked around an orderly universe dissolving into chaos and desperately needed a way to make sense of the pandemonium, to help people find each other when the official wires were cut, and to discover a voice that was not confined to a page.

Deniz peered from his attic at dark streets, candlelight like shy fireflies. He saw not an end but a bizarre beginning. His pirate signal, usually a whisper in electronic roar, was now a booming voice in the void. He needed to fill the quiet with more than echoes. The city was lost at sea. His untamed voice might be the only lifeboat.

Streets that had been rivers of light became echoing canyons. Paula stepped from her office; the click of her heels was swallowed. People wandered, bewildered, holding useless phones. Customer satisfaction meant nothing when customers could not find their way home. Wind whipped, carrying rain-scent and distant thunder. A storm was brewing in sky and hearts. If no one could shout directions or offer a steadying word, the city would be lost in the dark.

Deniz flicked on his battery-powered transmitter. The signal sputtered, a tiny spark against blackness.

“Ahoy, landlubbers,” he boomed, cheer not quite masking concern. “Looks like the big bad power company forgot to pay its bill. Or perhaps they’ve all gone to a really, really dark convention.” He knew it was more than a blackout. It was a test.

Paula tried to soothe a woman clutching a small child, voice wobbly around a practiced phrase: she understood this must be a difficult time; they were working to restore services. The words fell like pebbles into a well that led nowhere. The woman stared, worry Paula’s script could not touch. Genuine distress. A flush crept up Paula’s neck. Palms slick. She almost turned back to the empty office, the phantom comfort of a keyboard, a world where the only unpredictable element was a rogue paperclip.

Deniz pieced together fragmented whispers from other battery-powered radios, relaying warnings of traffic jams that had become stationary parking lots, blocked roads now impassable, people stranded far from home. His usual jokes wore a nervous energy, a way to keep his own spirits afloat as much as anyone else’s.

“So the city’s gone dark, eh?” he chuckled, though it sounded a little strained, like a rusty hinge. “Guess that means we all get to see the stars for a change. Hope you’ve got your astronaut helmets ready. But seriously, folks, keep your eyes peeled for signs of civilisation, and perhaps a working torch.” He broadcast instructions for finding safe havens, for conserving water, for looking out for neighbours. The attic smelled of biscuits and ozone. The transmitter was a tiny spark insisting it was still a city.

Then, from a small battery-powered radio clutched by a stranger huddled under a bus shelter, Paula heard it: a voice rough around the edges, full of spontaneous humour and surprisingly useful information. Deniz. He was directing people to a community centre that still had generators and a working kitchen, relaying messages from one confused neighbourhood to another, attempting to connect families separated by the sudden darkness. It was a glorious mess, a jumble of facts and jokes and urgent advice, but it was connection. Paula felt a strange jolt, a flicker of something she had not felt in years. This unscripted chaos was, in its own peculiar way, more comforting than any script she had ever written, more real than the polished phrases she had so carefully constructed. She had found her answer. The catch was clear: to help, she had to dive headfirst into that beautiful, terrifying mess and leave her scripts behind entirely.

She found the attic: wires, buzzing equipment, old coffee. Deniz grinned, hair standing as if he’d stuck a finger in a socket.

“You must be Paula. Heard you trying to soothe folks with your official-sounding voice on a neighbour’s radio. This city needs someone to untangle the mess.” He handed her a microphone, metal cool and slightly gritty. “You’re on. Tell me what you hear.”

Paula’s hand trembled as she grasped the microphone. To be brave meant letting go of the safety net of scripts, the familiar comfort of prepared words, and embracing the unknown of her own unscripted self. She hesitated, the weight of the microphone like an anchor. A gust rattled the attic window, a violent shake that made the radio equipment shudder, and the sharp wild smell of ozone filled the air. The transmitter crackled, a low ominous hum through the floorboards. Distant sirens, usually a comforting indicator of official response, now sounded like a mournful cry. The rough worn texture of the microphone felt alien after the smooth sterile plastic of her office headset. She took a deep, shaky breath that filled her lungs with dusty electric air, and spoke.

“Hello, city,” she said, voice surprisingly steady, a slight tremor undeniable. “This is Paula, and we’re going to get through this, together. Deniz has been gathering information, and we’re going to try and make it clear for everyone.”

Slowly, miraculously, the lights began to flicker back on, like shy stars appearing. The city, like a sleepy giant stirring, began to reawaken. Streetlights blinked, casting pools of familiar yellow onto damp pavement. Paula and Deniz, voices hoarse from hours of broadcasting, faces smudged with dust and sweat, watched official channels tentatively reappear on a small crackly screen. The quiet hum of electricity returned, but it was different now, softer, more appreciative, a sound that no longer went unnoticed. Paula left Deniz’s attic with the smell of old paper, static, and burnt toast clinging to her clothes, a scent that now smelled like courage. She was no longer the woman who hid behind carefully chosen words, who believed comfort came only from a script.

A few days later she was back in the training room. Fluorescent lights hummed, no longer oppressive. A new recruit, Kevin, nervous hands, furrowed brow, asked a question that was not in the manual: a customer utterly distraught over a lost package. Paula could have pulled the guide, promised a replacement in three to five business days. Instead she smiled, unscripted, crinkling the corners of her eyes.

“Ah, Kevin. That reminds me of a time the internet went out at my grandmother’s house during a terrible storm. We thought the world was ending. We ended up playing charades for three hours, laughing until our sides ached.”

She looked up at the lights. Once they had sounded like doom. Now they purred. A faint scent of ozone, once alarming, smelled like possibility.
characters: Paula (a call-center trainer), Deniz (the pirate-radio host)
